newsitem.title: USA: MSRB's upcoming rules get cautious market support.
newsitem.headline: MSRB's upcoming rules get cautious market support.

text.p: Municipal market leaders on Tuesday offered cautious support for the MSRB's upcoming raft of proposals to tighten disclosure by underwriters and financial advisers.

Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board officials announced on Monday that the panel will propose six rule changes before the end of the month that would require disclosure of syndicate practices, conflicts of interest and delivery of official bond sale statements.

"I think some of those things are worthy to be looked at," Arthur Heilman, chairman of the Government Finance Officers Association's committee on governmental debt and fiscal policy, said. "But I want to see what the regulatory format will be. As in anything, you can kill the market with regulation."

Heather Ruth, president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, said, "Over the years, the municipal bond industry has undertaken a number of initiatives to improve disclosure in the marketplace. Based on press reports, the (MSRB) proposals appear to be consistent with those initiatives."
"Our next step will be to carefully assess the practicality and potential impact of these disclosure proposals."

The MSRB said on Monday it will propose requiring underwriters and financial advisers to disclose to issuers whether they are acting as principals in "associated deals" such as swaps offerings and whether there are any third-party payments.

The board also said it would require underwriters to disclose issuer specifications for syndicate formation, bond allocations and other syndicate-related information. And it would require quicker settlement of syndicate accounts and require that bonds be allocated within 24 hours of a commitment wire.
Also, the board said it will propose requiring dealers to furnish regulators with the timing of their receipt of official statements from issuer clients in primary offerings.
Finally, the panel said it will seek comment on whether investors should be told when issuers select or "influence selection" of underwriter's counsel.
Catherine Spain, chief lobbyist for the Government Finance Officers Association, said the key issue for her group is whether the proposals are an improper intrusion on state and local governments.
"There is some sensitivity as to are they trying to regulate issuers," Spain said. "That will be a key point."
Spain said the proposal on OS delivery sounds reasonable.

"The suggestion there is that the issuers are not sending this stuff on time. I guess a lot of us have always thought why do (deal participants) go forward with a financing if they don't have the information," she asked.

"So maybe this is a good way to deal with it," said Spain, saying her views are personal and not necessarily those of GFOA. "I don't think you will see issuers defending issuers not providing information on a timely basis."
As for selection of underwriter's counsel by issuers, Spain said some issuers think that sometimes there are very good reasons for the issuer to dictate counsel.
"Maybe you are in the market so frequently that you just want to have the same counsel," she said.

Spain said her group wants to have "good airing" of the issues before taking a formal position. She said the proposals will be a key topic at the group's annual meeting in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., scheduled for the end of the month.
Meanwhile, two bond dealers that accused Washington regulators recently of overburdening the muni market with regulation were unavailable for comment.

Michael McCarthy, vice chairman of PSA and a managing director at Goldman, Sachs & Co., told PSA conferees earlier this year that new rules are laudable, but they are choking bond firms and not improving disclosure.
And R. Fenn Putman, chairman of O'Brien Partners, said that overzealous regulators are well meaning but getting "carried away," according to a report in The Bond Buyer.
Neither McCarthy or Putman was available for comment.
"I think we are anxious to see further detail," GFOA's Heilman said. "They (have said) they want to work us," he said, referring to MSRB. "We are certainly willing to do that."
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
